utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everybody in and around the courtroom. Barney Thomas, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and all in the courtroom and about the courtroom. Milos Androvic, Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I call you, Mr. Thomas, or do I call Mr. Cannata?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, me. Thank you. Before Dr. Mandilovic returns to continue with his testimony, there is a matter arising out of his testimony yesterday which I would want to raise before Your Honours. First of all, I hope Your Honours don't mind hearing from me instead of Mr. Cannata who led Dr. Mandilovic. I've made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just wondering why.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I've made my peace with him about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's made his peace with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, that's yet to be determined, actually. I hope we will get there. The issue concerns the basis upon which a number of exhibits were tendered. Particularly the distinction, if any, to be drawn between the ability to which or the extent to which Dr. Mandilovic could testify as to the truth of the contents of certain medical records, as against the ability of Your Honours to rely upon the contents of the medical records. The -- Your Honours will recall that there were a number of medical records admitted ultimately without objection and without -- without any conditions. And that there then began a process of admitting documents, medical records from medical facilities on certain conditions. The first time that these conditions were alluded to was in response or in the context of an objection made by my learned friend, and I'm referring, Your Honours, to page 4013 of yesterday's transcript at line 16. And if Your Honours don't have that available to you, I can read it into the record. Mr. Cannata attempted to tender as an exhibit 65 ter number 8692 and then Mr. Guy-Smith objected, and I'm quoting now from the transcript: "With regard to 65 ter 8692, to the extent that the document is being offered through this witness as an accurate reflection of records, there is no objection. To the extent this document is being offered with regard to the truth of the contents that is contained within these records, there is an objection." The response of Mr. Cannata was: "Your Honours. Yes, the Prosecution position is that Dr. Mandilovic is for these documents entitled to speak only to the -- to attest the accuracy and the validity and the fact that the documents, the medical records are authentic copies issued by the clinical centre. He will not give evidence as to the contents of the documents." And then my learned friend responds saying: "Understanding that they are not being offered for that purpose, I have no objection." Now, the critical point of my submission is that the Prosecution's position is that Mr. Mandilovic can't speak truth of the contents of these documents, and of course that's obvious, he wasn't involved in treating the patients concerned. Within that it had a series of documents being produced along largely formulaic lines such as my learned friend suggesting, for example, the next time a document was tendered for admission, and I'm quoting from line 17, page 4014: "If this document is being proposed under the same conditions as last document, there is no objection. Once again, not to speak to the truth of the contents contained in the document itself." The Prosecution agrees, and we have a number of documents being tendered in that way. So it would appear that the basis, the understood basis - at least on the record that these documents are going in - is that they have been authenticated by Dr. Mandilovic, but he himself personally cannot attest to the truth of the contents. The difficulty arises with the admission of the very last document of the session. And I'm quoting, Your Honours, from page 4017, beginning at line 8, and we are dealing with the final document of the day. Mr. Cannata moved for its admission, and my learned friend responded as follows, and this is at line 11 on page 4017: "With the same condition as the previous documents, there would be no objection, which is that he is not," and then he stopped and said "these documents are not being offered for the truth of the contents contained therein." Now, the difficulty, sir, is that that's the first time this formulation of these documents are not being offered for the truth of their contents appears on the record. There is a difference between Dr. Mandilovic not being able to attest to the truth of the contents and the documents themselves being evidence of the truth of their contents, as a record properly admitted for Your Honours to consider. It may be that Your Honours consider that you can rely on these documents for the truth of their contents, for demonstrating, for example, that a particular person was treated at a particular facility on a particular date. So the reason why I raise this is because there appears to be a conflict on the record in terms of the basis upon which these documents are being tendered. Because if they are being tendered on the basis that Your Honours simply can't consider them at all for the truth of their contents, then we have a difficulty because plainly that's not why they are being admitted. Also, this was not a formulation that appeared prior to the very last exhibit. And I wouldn't want to be in a position where any party is operating on the basis that Your Honours are not entitled to place whatever weight you wish upon the contents of these documents on the bases that they are properly admitted through Dr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is Mr. Cannata's response to that last formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Same conditions as before, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Mr. Thomas in his submission both misapprehends and misunderstands what the transcript says. Referring to the first time the objection came up, I say the following at page line [sic]. "To the extent this document is being offered with regard to the truth of the contents that is contained within these records, there is an objection." The next time I speak to it, which is at line 19, I say. "Understanding that they are not being offered for that purpose, the purpose being my original objection, the document being offered with regard to the truth of the contents that is contained within these records." And finally, the last time, I say: "With the same condition as the previous documents, there would be no objection." That is at page 417, which is that he is not, and then I say, as Mr. Thomas correctly points out "these document are not being offered for the truth of the contents contained therein." There is no difference between the meaning of with regard to the truth of the contents that is contained within these records, which is my very first objection, and the statement these documents are not being offered for the truth of the contents contained therein; although, it is not precisely the same language. It's certainly is exact same objection with the exact same intent and the Prosecution, in each and every time this was raised, made their position clear which was they were not offering the documents for the truth of the contents contained therein. So I do not share Mr. Thomas's perception or apprehension with regard to what was the Prosecution position with regard to the proffering of these documents. I recall that the Chamber at one point made it very clear to me, and I don't have the exact line, but that I should not tell the Prosecution how to prosecute its case. And I won't. But it's -- the objection is clear, the intent was clear from the beginning to the end, and the Prosecution agreed and made very clear what they were doing in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, my learned friends is right if one looks at his original objection and then the formulation which followed. But he misses a step, and I'm not suggesting for a moment that he wasn't justified or he isn't justified in taking the position that he takes now, but in my submission what I'm trying to alert Your Honours to is that plainly there are two different interpretations now occurring of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's precisely what your learned friend is contesting. He says that it's no different -- there are no different interpretations. Can I just read those two, just the two times that he raised the objections, the first one and the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just read them as they stand in the text? No, not now, there in that transcript that you have in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: He said: "With regard to 65 ter 8692, to the extent that the document is being offered through this witness as an accurate reflection of records, there is no objection. To the extent this document is being offered with regard to the truth of the contents that is contained within these records, there is an objection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's not where that exchange ends, however, Your Honour, but I will go to the last objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's where that objection arises. He says to the extent they are being tendered for the truthfulness of the contents there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what does the last one say?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The last one says: "With the same condition as the previous documents, there would be no objection, which is that he is not -- these document are not being offered for the truth of the contents contained therein."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the difference between that statement and the first statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The difference between that statement and the first statement is what happens immediately after the first statement, which that the response of the Prosecution to that first objection was this: "Your Honours. Yes, the Prosecution position is that Dr. Mandilovic is for these documents entitled to speak only to the -- to attest the accuracy and the validity and the fact that the documents, the medical records are authentic copies issued by the clinical centre. He will not give evidence as to the contents of the documents."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, Mr. Cannata misaddresses himself to the issue raised by the opposite side. Now, must the opposite side take blame for that? He is addressing what in his understanding Dr. Mandilovic can do. The objection is against the truthfulness of the contents of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I don't disagree with that, sir, but for the next response from Mr. Guy-Smith which was: "Understanding that they are not being offered for that purpose, I have no objection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, yeah, now we are getting into semantics.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The difficulty, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The difficulty here is that he is now misunderstanding --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata misunderstands him --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and he misunderstands Mr. Cannata to be agreeing with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we -- what relief do you ask for?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The relief I seek, sir, is that the Prosecution be entitled to tender the documents on the basis that it thought it was tendering them on. And that if my learned friend has an objection to that, that we hear argument on the objection and Your Honours rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just read. Mr. Guy-Smith, do you hear what the relief sought is, do you have any response to that? On the relief sought, not on the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I would argue against the relief sought because I don't share Mr. Thomas's -- what I consider to be Monday morning quarterbacking here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Monday morning quarterbacking. It's an American phrase dealing with -- there's always football game on Sunday, and on Monday there's an examination of the game, which is what I think is going on here. I believe that the procedure that was followed here, the objection is made, the proffer made by the Prosecution particularly in light of -- now, I'm speaking about what happened in a prior proceeding since he is a 92 ter witness, and this issue had been discussed in the Milosevic matter, and I alerted the Court to the pages of it, that it's inappropriate to be rehashing evidentiary rulings as we go along. There has to be some consistency of approach here. If we want to wipe the slate clean and start over again with the testimony of this particular witness, there are a series of other evidentiary issues that could have arisen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Can you confine yourself to the relief sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has listened to arguments on both sides, and has decided this is a matter that does not require any ruling in the court by the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber will attend to and address the arguments of the parties and interpret the documents in the light of the arguments that have been placed before it when it looks at the papers at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In which case, we can have Dr. Mandilovic brought in to continue his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may please sit down. Doctor, just to remind you, first of all, let me apologise to you for keeping you waiting until this time. We had said we will start at quarter past, but due to unforeseen circumstances and administrative matters that had to be attended to, we had to ask you to wait a little bit. Thank you very much. I see you are nodding. Just to remind you again that you are still by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you. Mr. Cannata, is it you or is it? Are we in cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith, that's you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I wasn't sure whether there were any last remarks Mr. Cannata wanted to make before I started based by the way we -- when we ended yesterday, I wasn't sure whether there were any last remarks or questions that Mr. Cannata had, but apparently I'm up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I understand your testimony, you are a specialist in a particular type of medicine; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is ENT; correct? And I'm going to ask you what ENT stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what does ENT stand for, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: ENT is ear, nose, throat. I am a surgeon, I've been a surgeon for a long time, specialising in head and neck surgery, and to be more specific, I specialise in the surgery of ear, nose, and throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the war started, that was also your specialty; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before the war started, did you work at the State Hospital? I'm sorry, you seem to have jumped to the microphone, so did I miss anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm okay. I'm perfectly okay. And I am all ears. I'm listening to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before the war started, did you work at the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the war started, was the State Hospital a civilian hospital or a military hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war started, it was a military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were working at the hospital before the war started, while it was a military hospital, were you working at the hospital as a civilian doctor or as a military doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a military doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was that a military doctor with the JNA or with some other military service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when you left the JNA before the war started?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you leave the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you left the JNA on the 2nd of May, 1992, did you have a particular rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that time I had a rank -- I apologise. I don't think you have phrased your question very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, then my apologies to you, let me rephrase my question. And I thank you for the correction. On the 2nd of May, 1992, when you left the JNA, what rank did you have in the JNA, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you left the JNA on the 2nd of May, 1992, as a major, did you have any difficulties in leaving the JNA? And by that I mean, did your commanding officer attempt to bar you from doing so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no problem, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a point this time when the military hospital became a civilian hospital in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military hospital was transformed into a civilian hospital on the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the time that the military hospital was transformed into a civilian hospital on the 10th of May, 1992, were the supplies that were at the hospital taken from the hospital by the JNA? I'm sorry, that's assuming something that I perhaps should not assume. On the 10th of May, 1992, when the hospital transformed into a civilian hospital, did the JNA militarily leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA did leave the hospital but they did not take any medical supplies, equipment, or prescription drugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it by that it would be fair to assume that when the hospital metamorphised from a military hospital into a state hospital, it was in such a state as to continue engaging in medical work; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fairly complex question. There was equipment, certain material because equipment, supplies in the medical sense, replenished periodically. We can't claim that when the JNA left the hospital that it didn't take anything with it, that's correct, but we didn't have many supplies. There were supplies only for a certain period of time, so we could conditionally say that the newly transformed hospital continued with its work, but it couldn't work with the existing supplies for a lengthy period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. When the JNA left the hospital and the hospital transformed into a civilian hospital, did you remain in essentially the same position that you had been in while the hospital had been a military hospital? And by that I mean the head of the department of the ENT?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In professional terms I maintained the position that I had. However, not in medical terms --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter heard the witness correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in medical terms what occurred is -- would it be fair to say what occurred in medical terms is that your duties were expanded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duties, I'm talking about my professional duties, were expanded. With time the war escalated, there were more wounded and sick people, and therefore my medical duties were expanded. That's the case in every war. I was no longer just a specialist, surgical specialist for ENT. I had to become involved in other medical duties as well. I wasn't just an ear, nose, and throat specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did your duties include maintaining hospital records? And by that I mean, did you personally maintain hospital records for the entire State Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I had absolutely nothing to do with the records maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you continue to be the head of a department which maintained records within the hospital administration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was he ever the head of a department which maintained records?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I got ahead of myself. I'll ask the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you ever the head of a department which maintained records, and I perhaps in that regard --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I'm an ear, nose, and throat surgeon. I was the head of the ward that was involved exclusively in treating ear, nose, and throat illnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you maintain as the head of the department for ear, nose -- as an ear, nose, and throat surgeon particular protocols with regard to the activities that you performed at the State Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you the custodian of those records, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for one year. Later, these records were handed over to the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the records that you have testified about here, are those records that you brought with you when you testified in the very first case that you came to testify to, and by that I mean did you bring those records physically with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't have any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry, Doctor. Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, can I have a qualification. Those records -- well, Dr. Mandilovic testified about documents which were tendered in the Dragan Milosevic case, and I take that my learned friend referred to that -- his testimony in the Galic case, when he says at page 16, line 5 when he says, "You testified in the very first case." Now, can I have clarification --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regards to the records that you testify to concerning the Milosevic case, are those records that you brought with you when you came to testify in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, I didn't bring any documents with me. It wasn't even possible for me to obtain those medical documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The documents that you testified to in the Milosevic case, and the documents that you have testified to in this case came from, as I understand it, two separate hospital entities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One hospital entity was the State Hospital where you worked; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the other hospital entity is a hospital where you did not work; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of records, am I correct in my understanding that records are contained in what could be called a hospital book?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, hospital protocol, that's what we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And am I correct also that the -- one of the hospital that you mentioned in your testimony yesterday went by another name and that is the name Kosevo Hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Kosevo Clinical Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the medical records from the Kosevo Hospital, you testified in a prior proceeding in the Milosevic case, I refer the Court and counsel to page 577, lines 1 through 4 as follows to the following question asked by you -- asked of you by the Prosecution: "Q. And with respect to hospital medical records from the Kosevo Hospital, did you ever have occasion to see such records?" And your answer was: "Of course, very often. I don't mean their actual hospital books and records, but I did see on many occasions their medical reports and findings by their physicians." Do you maintain that testimony as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have -- if we could have I think it's 65 ter 09244 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, during the period of time that you were working as a doctor in Sarajevo, were you aware of the fact that there was a tunnel that existed by which people could leave the city?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That tunnel, if you have the tunnel beneath the airstrip in mind, that tunnel was constructed in the course of the war. You say that people were able to leave the town, but the tunnel was under strict control. It wasn't easy to pass through the tunnel. It was used for the army, the Bosnian army. They could pass through the tunnel and supplies could be taken through the tunnel, but private individuals couldn't use the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. My apologies, I understand. The tunnel that existed when you say it was under the control of the army, is -- did you ever -- first of all, did you ever go to this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you, in your position at the hospital, receive any medical supplies from the army that came through the tunnel, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know how the hospital found medical supplies, how it obtained those supplies. I can't be certain, but I think that to a large extent the French Battalion, the French forces under UNPROFOR that were in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time provided them with supplies. As for the tunnel, well, I really don't know. I'm not familiar with those details, I wasn't involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that during your tenure at the hospital, during the war years - and I'm referring to the war years - that you did receive supplies from UNPROFOR from -- no matter whether they be French or other parts of UNPROFOR, and by that I mean other nationalities who are part of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, but although I have all the goodwill that is needed, I can't answer your question. I didn't involve myself in that field. I didn't have such authority and I wasn't involved in that. I was only involved in professional matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. If we can't take it any further, we shan't take it any further. If you could take a look at the map here, and I know it's kind of small and if we need to make it bigger, I'm happy to do that. Looking at this map can you, first of all, recognise this as being a map of, what I would say is Sarajevo and central Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a map of Sarajevo, but it's not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the map in its present condition, can you identify on the map where the State Hospital is that you worked at, or would it be better if it was enlarged, because we can enlarge the map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if you could enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Without enlarging it in gross, is there some specific portion of the map that would be helpful to be enlarged? And you'll notice there are a number of longitudinal and latitudinal lines on the map also which create boxes. So starting on the left-hand side of the map, if we count the number of box, would it be helpful to enlarge some particular part of it for you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be useful if we could zoom in and enlarge the central part where there is a lot of black, a little further to the left, just the central part of the town. A little lower down. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you like to go the other way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About here. No, here. I think you've gone too far aware. Try and enlarge this part. Stop there. Could you scroll a bit to the right, this is not the area. No, to the other side. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at this part of the map, is -- are you able to identify using this map where the State Hospital would be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can we get assistance from the usher now, then. I'm going to have the usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's here. It's about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could mark the area where the hospital is with an H for hospital. Great, you circle and if you mark, make it an SH for State Hospital. Good. H will work.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SH, SH.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] State Hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Now, with regard to the position of the State Hospital, between September of 1992 and spring of 1993 using this particular map, can you -- can you help us with where the confrontation lines were to the east of the hospital, assuming that I'm accurate with regard to there being confrontation line east of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you are right, sir. The main problem for the State Hospital came from the south. That's from the Trebevic mountains, the Jewish cemetery, Grbavica, from that direction. That was the main problem, the limits, the borders to the east, the lines to the east were quite far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of what I have said, you could also make use of -- some photographs of the hospital would show that the destruction was greatest south of the hospital, and the destruction was not that significant on the other sides, in the other directions from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt. Can I have a correction on the transcript, maybe we can re-ask the same question to the witness. Page 21, line 2, I understood from the translation that it was Mount Trebevic page 21, line 2. And that it not accurately reported in the transcript, can we have it clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll have to go back to the audio, because I'm not positive that Mr. Cannata is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 2, as I read it says: "I don't think you are right, sir --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. "I don't think you are right, sir. The main problem for the state," that's line 2. Then line 3 continues: "Hospital came from the south, that's interest the Trebevic," and then something is missed, and then "... mountains, the Jewish cemetery," and then something is missed, "... that was the problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have page 21, line 2, and my point is that the mountains, Trebevic, is not the correct interpretation. At this stage if it cannot be clarified, I would ask the audiotape to be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, it can be clarified. The question can be put back to the witness and he can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If it's a point of a need of clarification, I'm happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I believe you can just ask the question again, let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, there seems to be some confusion with regard to the issue of the mountain. Could you kindly tell us which mountain it is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, of course. The Trebevic mountain, the slopes of the Trebevic mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, if we could have this map as the defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That document shall be given Exhibit number D59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm done with that map at this time. We can take it off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to see whether or not the following is correct because perhaps I'm misunderstanding your testimony, sir. And I'm referring the Court and counsel to page 1014 and 1015 of the Galic trial. Starting at line 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have the Galic trial transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust that you do. I'm going to read it verbatim. You don't? Great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, was it distributed? Was it disclosed to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. It was and it is P632. It's P632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P632. P632, are you calling that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right, because you asked whether you had it or not, and I'm noting it's P632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page 1014, which I believe is page 8 of 26 in the electronic version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that's the exhibit you are calling, P632?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked the following question and gave the following answer, and that's with regard to issue of the confrontation to the east, which is: "Q. Were there any other confrontation lines in that -- well, close to the hospital, say on the east, the west, or the north? "A. Yes, of course there were. Yes, because the city of Sarajevo is not a large city in terms of space, and these were mostly in the old part of town, the centre of town, and parts closer to the old part of town so that in practical terms, towards the east is the end of town which is encircled by the mountains. And so quite certainly towards the east of the hospital there were military conflicts going on." First of all, just with regard to the directional issue: Is the statement that you made in the Galic trial in response to a question by the Prosecutor concerning conflicts accurate, that there were military conflicts east of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, there's something I would like to explain to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, you are more than welcome to explain any answer that you wish to give, but I have a specific question with regard to your prior testimony in a proceeding before the Tribunal when the issue of the direction and the confrontation lines came up. So my first question is, is this testimony accurate, the answer that you gave in the Galic case an accurate answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I understand that you wish to explain something. Is what you wish to explain with regard to the issue of direction, by that I mean north, south, east, or west?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, with your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely, I have no desire to inhibit your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Sir, in one of your previous questions you asked me where the most frequent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness didn't end the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that Sarajevo is fairly small town surrounded by mountains. It was fully encircled and there was fighting ongoing on all sides. There's no dilemma about. However, if you ask me where the most frequent attacks on the hospital came from, then the answer is from the south. If you have photographs from prior -- previous periods from other trials that you can see those photographs that show the destruction, terrible destruction on that side. The building is a 12-floor building, and naturally it was hit by shells from other directions since it was totally encircled, but the southern side was the most exposed side. That's what I wanted to say. I didn't participate in the fighting, you know. I didn't plan the fights either. There was ongoing fighting on all sides. There was fighting when we tried to overcome the enemy and so on and so forth. So there was the hospital devastation that shouldn't be confounded or mixed up with the fighting that was ongoing to the east, to the west, to the south, in relation to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question -- and I appreciate your answer, thank you for that. My question is, with regard to confrontation lines, was there a confrontation line east of the hospital, and if I understand your testimony, the answer to that question is, Yes, there was. I'll follow that up with the following question, which is: Could you tell the Chamber -- excuse me, could you tell the Chamber about how far in distance from the hospital that confrontation line was to the east in the time-period of 1992 through 1993? Can you give us that information, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be really very precise, but I can put it this way, sir. The eastern confrontation line was relatively far from the hospital. I'm talking about the eastern confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "relatively far," could you give us an estimate in metres? Was it 200 metre, 300, 400 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, sir. It was much further. What we are talking about, what I testified about earlier was the frontline in the south direction which was some 3- or 400 metres as the crow flies, and as for the eastern frontline, it was several kilometres away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. Are you able to estimate how many kilometres to the east the frontline was? If you are not able to, you are not able to. But if you say it's in kilometres, it's got to be sort of in kilometres rather than metres, then we also understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, not in metre. It was certainly several kilometres in the direction east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you say 10 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, less, less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you say 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3 to 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's just what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the confrontation line that was south of the hospital, that confrontation line, if I understand your testimony correctly, was some 3- to 400 metres from the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, yes, and that would be my free estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 09244 back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm always concerned when you put up the map when it's been drawn on. I never know which way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again looking at this map here, can you draw, with the assistance of the usher, where the confrontation line was south of the hospital that you indicated was some 3- to 400 metres south of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, providing you blow up that section of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll see what we can do for you in that regard, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same zone that I was supposed to mark just a couple of minutes ago. [In English] Can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is the area that you have marked with a circle, the area that you were telling us was where the confrontation line was? Or is that where the hospital was? I think the circle is where the hospital is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. No, you're mistaken. The hospital is more to the north from that. I can also draw the place or mark the place where the hospital was. May I do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Great. Could you mark the top circle with an SH for State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you mark that, the bottom circle, with a CL for confrontation line, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have that admitted as Defence next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The exhibit is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number D60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, did I ask that it be marked? D60. Are you done, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, I said, "Thank you very much for your time, sir." I should have said, I'm completed. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you did say but I was talking to the Judge on this side. Any re-examination, Mr. Cannata?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question, Doctor. It seems to me that you said in your testimony that the shots came from the Jewish cemetery of Sarajevo which is on the other side of the river with regard to the hospital. And now on the map that you have just marked and showed the confrontation line, you put the confrontation line on the same side as the hospital, so I'm a bit lost with regard to that. I may be mistaken, I don't know. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I didn't. I made sure to do everything properly. There is another confrontation line, and where I marked was the place where the Jewish cemetery was, and the river is still between the two. And if the cross does not denote the Jewish cemetery, then I'm mistaken, but I thought that the cross on the map denotes the Jewish cemetery and that's what I went by. I must tell you that the distances on the map are really very very small. It's a small place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you properly, the confrontation line was on the other side of the river vis-a-vis to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If I can follow up on your question and the statement by the lawyer, I'm not happy with the "confrontation line," with that term. It's actually the position of the troops of the Army Republika Srpska from which one part of the city was controlled. I believe that this would be a better definition. I'm sorry if I have offended somebody with proffering my definition, but I think that the term is much better and much clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, now I don't understand what you are saying. I apologise. I just wanted to clarify things, I was a bit confused. So according to you, the confrontation line was on the other bank of the river which is [indiscernible] by the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because on the map, the way you marked you put the confrontation line on the same bank as the hospital, so I suppose that you just made a little mistakes. And I agree with you that the plan is very small, that the map is small.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I made a mistake, I apologise. The map is indeed small, but as I've already tried to explain, I was governed by the mark of the cross which represented the Jewish cemetery and that is on the southern bank -- bank of the river. There is no dilemma about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I believe that now the matters are absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the Judge's questions, Mr. Cannata?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I only, for purposes of clarification, I perhaps am a bit confused. I don't know if it's of any help to the Chamber to have the map redrawn or not. I am happy to do that if that's something that the Chamber believes would be of assistance, but if the Chamber is satisfied with the testimony as it stands, then I'll just leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't decide for you when you ask questions arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, then I have no further questions, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You can -- every once in awhile you can help me out a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but not how to conduct your trial. I beg your pardon, Doctor, thank you so much for taking the time from your very busy schedule to come and testify at the Tribunal. This brings us now to the conclusion of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down, and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata, you think you can finish the next witness in the next three minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I will because I'm not leading the next witness, Your Honours. Mr. Thomas will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, would that be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I would say, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I call Mr. Vejzagic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mister?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Vejzagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it a mister?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mister, sir, yes. Who is also a 92 ter witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Are you comfortably settled there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you, yes, I am quite comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you begin, sir, by telling us your full name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Nedzad Vejzagic, I was born on the 2nd of July, 1948 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: I am a currently a retired former employee of the Ministry of Interior Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And are you a forensic scientist investigator by trade?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: I spent my whole career as a forensic expert in the laboratories of the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall giving an interview to myself and other members of the Office of the Prosecutor in April of last year?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please have 65 ter 09400 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise, sir, the -- that is the statement that you gave to us at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document that I signed on the 25th of April, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And is that your signature which we see on the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity over the last few days to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've had the opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are the contents of the statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: It's the statement that I signed on the 25th of April, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are the assertions you've made in that statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: The assertions that I made at the time, I believe, are true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And if I asked you the same questions today that you were asked during that interview, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: I would adhere by the same words.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If the statement could please be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement includes a schedule of around 50 documents which were reviewed for the purposes of the statement which have also comprised the 92 ter -- or the exhibits to be tendered as part of the 92 ter package. No comment is required in respect of those exhibits other than one or two matters of clarification which I can deal with generally following the tendering of those exhibits. I've discussed both with the madam case officer and my learned friends whether there is a way we can do this without calling up each exhibit individually in court, and I'm told that if I signal -- that one option, depending on how Your Honours wish to proceed, is that we can simply instruct Madam Registrar to assign P number to the exhibits listed in the 92 ter package, except in the case of two or three where some further comment is required. If Your Honours are prepared to proceed on that basis, we avoid the process of having to assign P numbers to all 50 of those Exhibits during the sitting of the Court. But I'm in Your Honours hands as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Their Honours are in your colleague's hands on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is the agreement that Mr. Thomas and I worked out with regard to this specific witness and these particular exhibits, all of which I believe Mr. Thomas would acknowledge are unscheduled incidents in terms of -- one of the meanings that we have for unscheduled incidents in terms of this case. And by that I mean they are not found in the indictment. I may be incorrect, there may be one that is found in the indictment, but apart from that -- apart from that issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without characterising the nature of the exhibits, what is the position of the Defence with regard to the admissibility as a batch?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from that issue that I just mentioned, I have made an agreement with Mr. Thomas with regard to these documents, and they can all be assigned a P number as suggested by Mr. Thomas. If the Chamber wishes to proceed along those lines as opposed to -- as opposed to -- excuse me, you know what, I just understood in a different fashion precisely what your question is, and I'm going to answer precisely what your question is. I agree with Mr. Thomas, and I would suggest to the Court what we do in this instance is we assign P number to each and every one of the documents at the convenience of the Registrar without further adieu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In which case the record should probably reflect that P numbers be assigned as per the 92 ter package except for 65 ter 08320.01, which is in the package but which the Prosecution does not seek to tender. Also a P number does not need to be assigned to 07200. That has already been assigned an exhibit number of P468. And in respect of 65 ter 08320.13, the Prosecution wishes to tender only pages 19 and 20 of the B/C/S version, and the attached three page English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, at the convenience of the Registrar outside court hours, can you please assign Exhibit numbers to all those documents according to the suggestion of Mr. Thomas as mentioned in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will do, Your Honours. Internal memoranda will be distributed to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Madam Registrar, and thank you to my learned friends. Sir if I may be permitted at this strategic read a very brief summary of Mr. Vejzagic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Vejzagic is forensic scientist, now retired. From 1974 until 2006, he worked in that capacity for the Federal Ministry of the Interior for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Sarajevo, which was responsible for investigating serious crimes including shelling incidents. He was head of the forensic department from 1999 until 2001, and was engaged in that capacity in Sarajevo throughout the war. Mr. Vejzagic describes the method of investigation and the manner of preparation of investigation reports. He reviewed a number of reports related to shelling incidents where 120 millimetre mortar shells landed and exploded in ABiH held parts of the city. The reports detail, inter alia, the recovery of shell fragments from the impacts sites. These fragments bear the markings of the manufacturer and the dates of production. The manufacturer was the Krusik factory in Valjevo, Serbia, and the period during which the components concerned were manufactured was 1993 to 1995. Mr. Vejzagic also comments upon periods of every day shelling and incessant sniping of civilians by forces of the Bosnian Serb army positioned on high ground surrounding the city. And finally, Your Honour, there are some matters of clarification arising from his statement and the exhibits referred to which I would like to go through briefly with Mr. Vejzagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, many of the reports you reviewed related to components of a 120-millimetre mortar shell. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And you also refer in your statement to a manual which depicts, among other things, a 120-millimetre mortar shell and its various components, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask to you just describe in general terms what a 120-millimetre mortar shell is and what it is comprised of. And if it assists you, I'd like to provide you with the corresponding page from the manual --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: -- which, if we could have on the screens, Your Honour, is 65 ter number 08747. Page 2 of the original B/C/S version, please, and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, you should have on the screen there a diagram of an artillery shelf some description. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Either with reference to that diagram, if it assists you, or otherwise, could you please describe to Their Honours the various components of a 120-millimetre mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to call myself an expert for this type of shells; however, I am familiar with certain things because during my service in the JNA I became familiar with such tools. For in general terms here, I can see that this shell consists of a body. There is a detonator, and then the bottom part is also known as the shell tail with some openings and wings, which stabilise the shell during its trajectory. And as far as I can remember, within the body of the mine, there is the explosive charge, and on its top is a detonator which is impact prone, and when the shell falls on a hard service, it is detonated and shell explodes, i.e., the charge that is within the body of the shell explodes. The bottom part of the shell is also known as the shell tail. There are stabilising wings, and something which you don't see on the image, there is another charge that detonates the gunpowder that propels the shell through the barrel. The shell is detonated when the -- when a member of the crew puts the shell in the barrel. It travels through the barrel, it hits the detonator, and then the gunpowder is ignited and jets the shell out of the barrel. The range of these shells depends on the angle of the barrel from which the shell is propelled. The bigger the angle, the shorter the range. The smaller the angle, the further the range, and it also depends on the quantity of the gun part charge. This is as much as I can see on the image, helped with what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, just before you proceed and just for the record, can we just clarify the capacity in which the witness is coming. He described himself as not an expert in these things. I see according to the witness list that he is a crime base witness, but we have been given his CV, which suggested to me he is coming as an expert. I'm also confused. I would like to know exactly what his status is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: His status, Your Honour, is this something you'd you want to hear from me answer or get some clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what witness you called in him. Did you call an expert witness or did you call a crime base witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No. I called an investigator to tender investigation reports, Your Honour. So I'm simply because the reports refer to certain components, I simply wish to provide some assistance through him of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted -- indeed. I just wanted to know now that he put a caveat at the beginning, he said that he doesn't call himself an expert in these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand, sir. It wasn't an intention to lead that as expert testimony. More as background information for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, there are just a couple of things I would like to ask you about what you've just told us. You mentioned the tail-fin of the shell, and you also later on mentioned the stabilising fin. Are these the same thing or different things?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: At the tail of the shell, the cylindrical part with the holes, you have these fins and that's called a stabiliser, you know -- stabilise the shell stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. There is reference in the reports to the stabiliser, and there's also reference in the reports to what is known as the basic charge or primary charge. Where we see those references, what would that refer to?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: To the gunpowder charge in the shell. If you want a greater range, you add gunpowder and that thereby increases the shell's range.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter number 47 -- 87 -- I'll start again. 08746 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I take it 08747, page 3, has therefore already been tendered --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- in that batch?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It has, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you will recognise this as a photograph attached to one of the reports that you reviewed for the purposes of your statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you identify for us the two items that we see on the left-hand side of the image?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: We can see the shell tail and the stabilising fins and below we can see -- well, we can see an opening on the tail. And this part should have been there, that is the detonator cap. You can see that a pin was used to fire this. The parts to the right, metal pieces from the shell, and there are other parts that should have filled in the tail of the shell and should have plugged it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I wonder if I can ask for the assistance of Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: With the assistance of this pen, sir, can you please draw a circle around the item that you describe as the detonator cap.

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: So this part is placed here. So this is the cap. It's at the bottom of the shell. When the shell is put into the barrel, this cap is then ignited here. This is where it is ignited by the pin at the bottom of the barrel. These parts here are the felt plugs that are inside the shell, and inside that cartridge you also have the charge, the gunpowder charge, which is covered by these felt plugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Just pause for a moment. You mentioned that the charge is inside the cartridge. Where is the cartridge? Do we see it or any part of it in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: This cap has a lower part that is missing. It's similar to the cartridge used for a hunting rifle. So it's between 7 and 10 centimetres long usually, then you have a gunpowder charge inside the felt plugs in at the top, and they prevent the gunpowder charge from spilling out. Here you have the cap, you have the cap, when it's hit by the firing pin, a flame is created and this sets fire to the gunpowder charge through the hole that we saw awhile ago, or from that hole the gunpowder gas can come out, and they in fact discharge the shell from the barrel and fire it over a certain range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It seems that the witness is being called to testify at this point as an expert, not as a fact witness with regard to investigation reports, and I would object on those grounds at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you say he is being called as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because he is explaining to us a series of matters that certainly are beyond the ken of someone who is a forensic investigator but are dealing now specifically with the specific discipline of artillery and firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, sir, he is not giving any sort of opinion. So that's point number one. The second point, sir, is that the weight to be attached to the testimony that is he now giving is a matter for Your Honours. This is evidence that's within his experience. It's -- it should be taken for what it is. The observations of an investigator whose experience is limited to investigating in the manner described in the statement. Of course he can't testify as to how shells are fired in the same way that an artillery expert could testify, but he is trained in the collection of evidence, and all I'm attempt tempting to do, for Your Honours, is to give names to the fragments that are found and referred to in the reports. And that is the reason for this evidence and that is the only extents to which the evidence can reasonably be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I reiterate what the witness said right at the beginning, that he doesn't regard himself as an expert in this and, indeed, that's how I was viewing his testimony. However, my concern, which is slightly different from Mr. Guy-Smith's concern, is that the witness is now drawing new parts instead of describing the parts that are photographed. That's my concern. And I was just wondering whether the part he is drawing, don't you have it in subsequent pictures where he can talk about that there. And I would have expected you to stop him from drawing but rather just to tell us what these things are because that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, sir. I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. And in fact I propose that he redraw. I thought that the evidence would still be of some assistance to Your Honours, but I can limit it to what's on the screen. And we'll start again which I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine or I would expect that what he draws you do have in picture for him in some other exhibit, and you'll get to that exhibit and he can tell us that instead of drawing it here. And if you don't have it, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. All right. Madam Registrar, can we please have a clean version of that exhibit up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, can you please just draw a circle around the item that you have identified as the detonator for the charge, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: That's the detonator.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you draw a line from there straight down towards the bottom of the picture and mark a D next to that line, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle around the remnants of the charge that you have described, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: This should be a, what's it called, the cartridge, the cardboard cartridge, and the length should be about 10 centimetres. It's similar to the cartridge used for a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, just pause. We understand that. Please just draw the circle around the remnants of the charge. And if you've completed that, just say so.

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you draw a C next to that marking, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you then draw an arrow pointing to that part of the stabiliser which the charge is inserted into?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And finally, sir, the reports mention markings that are found on the charge or on the stabiliser throughout the reports that you reviewed, can you just draw a line or indicate in some way where you would see those markings in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And could you please put an arrow head at the end of the line where you see the markings?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Your Honours, can we please tender that as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The picture is it admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P646.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Madam Registrar. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, now, I just want to clarify some language that is used in some of the reports. The reports refer to the aggressor or the aggressor's positions. Which force is denoted by the term "aggressor," or whose positions are denoted by the terms "aggressor's positions"?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: The term "aggressor" or "aggressor positions" refer to the positions of the VRS. The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And finally there are a number of locations referred throughout the reports that I'd just like you to identify for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could please have Exhibit P370 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: 370. Well, we don't want the marked map, Your Honour, and my apologies if that's a marked map. Then, can we please have 65 ter number 09244 on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: First of all, sir, do you recognise that as a map of Sarajevo and its surrounds?

utterances.speaker: NEDZAD VEJZAGIC
utterances.text: I can see that this is Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
